books.title: The Two-Sen Copper Coin
books.author: Edogawa Rampo
books.synopsis: A gentleman thief hides a stolen 50,000 yen, and two poor roommates fall to decoding a cryptic note of dots and dashes made from a copper coin's secret message. When one of them thinks he has cracked it and fetches the loot, the other reveals the whole thing was his elaborate prank.

books.title: The Human Chair
books.author: Edogawa Rampo
books.synopsis: A famous woman novelist opens a bundle of manuscript pages from a stranger and reads a chilling confession: a homeless furniture maker once hid inside a leather armchair and lived in it, feeling the bodies of those who sat on it. A second letter arrives to say that he wrote the story for her.

books.title: The Stalker in the Attic
books.author: Edogawa Rampo
books.synopsis: Bored and fascinated only by crime, lodger Saburo discovers he can crawl through the ceiling space above his boarding house and spy on his neighbors through the boards. His game turns deadly when he drips morphine through a knot-hole onto a hated fellow lodger, and the detective Akechi Kogoro sees through him.

books.title: Beast in the Shadows
books.author: Edogawa Rampo
books.synopsis: A detective novelist meets the beautiful wife of a businessman, who is being blackmailed by the reclusive horror writer Oe Shundei, her former lover. When the husband is found drowned and the letters keep coming, the narrator is drawn into a hunt where every clue seems lifted from Shundei's own stories.

books.title: The Strange Tale of Panorama Island
books.author: Edogawa Rampo
books.synopsis: Hitomi Hirosuke, a penniless writer who dreams of building his own utopia, discovers he is the double of a dead millionaire and takes his place after digging up the grave. With the fortune he builds a vast artificial island of panoramas, fireworks and underwater wonders, until a former colleague sees through him.

books.title: The Black Lizard
books.author: Edogawa Rampo
books.synopsis: The female master thief Black Lizard announces she will steal the Star of Egypt, a priceless diamond owned by the jeweler Iwase, and kidnaps his daughter Sanae to get it. Only the great detective Akechi Kogoro can match her in a duel of disguises, traps and nerve.

books.title: The Tattoo
books.author: Jun'ichirō Tanizaki
books.synopsis: In old Edo, the tattooist Seikichi has spent years searching for a woman whose skin is worthy of his soul's masterpiece. When a teenage geisha apprentice arrives, he drugs her and inks a giant black widow spider across her back, and she wakes transformed, making him her first victim.

books.title: Naomi
books.author: Jun'ichirō Tanizaki
books.synopsis: Jōji, a sober Tokyo engineer, takes a fifteen-year-old café waitress named Naomi into his home to mould her into the perfect Westernized wife. She grows into a capricious, scornful beauty with a string of dancing-hall lovers, and he ends up her willing slave, grovelling on all fours for her favours.

books.title: A Portrait of Shunkin
books.author: Jun'ichirō Tanizaki
books.synopsis: A narrator pieces together the story of Shunkin, a blind, imperious Osaka shamisen master, from a slim memorial biography and local memory. Her devoted servant Sasuke becomes her pupil and lover, and after a night attacker scars her face he pierces his own eyes with a needle so he will never see her ruined.

books.title: Some Prefer Nettles
books.author: Jun'ichirō Tanizaki
books.synopsis: Kaname and his wife Misako drift toward a divorce neither can bring herself to name, while his old father-in-law indulges in a Kyoto mistress and the puppet theatre of Osaka. Torn between modern Tokyo tastes and the old Kansai ways, Kaname finds himself drawn to the doll-like Ohisa and the slow, graceful traditions she embodies.

books.title: Diary of a Mad Old Man
books.author: Jun'ichirō Tanizaki
books.synopsis: Seventy-seven-year-old Utsugi, ailing and half-paralysed, records in his diary his obsessive lust for his son's glamorous wife Satsuko, who toys with him and extracts silk scarves and jewels in return for small intimacies. He plans to have her sole carved on his gravestone like a Buddha's footprint stone, so that he can feel her tread on him after death.

books.title: Dogra Magra
books.author: Yumeno Kyūsaku
books.synopsis: A man wakes in a cell of a Kyushu university asylum with no memory of who he is, while two rival professors feed him a cursed manuscript, a ghastly murder case and a theory of ancestral dreams. Each document overturns the last in a looping, maddening labyrinth of mind and heredity.

books.title: The Crab Cannery Ship
books.author: Kobayashi Takiji
books.synopsis: Fishermen and boys hired in Hakodate are shipped to the Okhotsk Sea aboard the rotting factory ship Hakkō Maru, where the overseer Asakawa drives them to sickness and death for the company's profit. Beaten down and finally pushed to strike, the men learn what organization means.

books.title: The Wind Has Risen
books.author: Hori Tatsuo
books.synopsis: A writer follows his fiancée Setsuko, who is dying of tuberculosis, to a mountain sanatorium, where they spend a hushed last season together watching her paintings and the seasons fade. After her death he spends a snowbound winter alone in a mountain cabin, reading and writing to come to terms with the loss.

books.title: The Book of the Dead
books.author: Orikuchi Shinobu
books.synopsis: In eighth-century Nara, a noble's daughter copying the Pure Land sutra a thousand times is drawn to a mountain temple at Taima by the vision of a figure in the sunset. Meanwhile a long-entombed prince, a royal ghost, wakes in his dark tomb, calling for the woman he loved.

books.title: On Decadence
books.author: Sakaguchi Ango
books.synopsis: Writing in the ruins of defeated Japan, Ango argues that the kamikaze pilots turning into black marketeers and the war widows taking new lovers are simply humans returning to themselves. Bushido and the emperor system were devices against human weakness, and people must fall all the way down to find their own salvation.

books.title: The Golden Demon
books.author: Ozaki Kōyō
books.synopsis: Hazama Kan'ichi, a poor student raised in the Shigisawa household, is betrothed to their daughter Miya until the wealthy Tomiyama dazzles her with diamonds and a rich marriage. Crushed and furious, Kan'ichi throws away his studies and becomes a ruthless moneylender, while Miya's regret pours out in long, unanswered letters.

books.title: The Broken Commandment
books.author: Shimazaki Tōson
books.synopsis: Segawa Ushimatsu, a respected schoolteacher in Nagano, hides that he was born into the outcast burakumin class, bound by his father's one commandment: never reveal it. Drawn to the writings and courage of the openly outcast thinker Inoko Rentarō, he moves into a temple lodging and wrestles with the confession that will cost him everything.

books.title: Musashino
books.author: Kunikida Doppo
books.synopsis: A narrator living in a thatched hut near Shibuya walks the oak woods and fields of the Musashino plain through autumn and winter, quoting his diary for the sound of wind in the leaves, the low sun and the quiet. He finds the poetry of a place in its crossroads, village edges and small streams, and in a Russian birch wood he first learned to hear.

books.title: The Quilt
books.author: Tayama Katai
books.synopsis: Takenaka Tokio, a thirty-something writer weary of his marriage, takes in the bright young Yoshiko as his literary disciple and falls painfully in love with her. When her sweetheart Tanaka follows her to Tokyo, Tokio's jealousy, drinking and hypocrisy spiral until he sends her home.

books.title: A Country Teacher
books.author: Tayama Katai
books.synopsis: Seizō, a middle-school graduate from Gyōda who dreams of poetry and a literary career, takes a post at a village school in Saitama and lodges at a temple in Hanyū. Over the years friendships fade, love goes nowhere, debts and illness close in, and the Russo-Japanese War rumbles on while he wastes away teaching in the country.

books.title: Nogiku no Haka
books.author: Itō Sachio
books.synopsis: Looking back more than ten years, Masao recalls growing up in a farmhouse at Yagiri with his cousin Tamiko, two years his elder, whose easy closeness is spoiled when the household gossips. Sent away to school, he learns too late that Tamiko was married against her will and died holding his photograph and letter, and he lays wild chrysanthemums on her grave.

books.title: Vita Sexualis
books.author: Mori Ōgai
books.synopsis: Professor Kanai, a philosophy lecturer who has never written a book, decides to set down the history of his own sexual life, so that he might one day show it to his grown-up son. He recalls his boyhood from the age of six, from lending-library romances and a stolen peek at a bawdy picture book to dormitory crushes and a half-awakened feeling for the maid Ochō, down to his first visit to a teahouse as a young doctor.

books.title: Sanshō the Bailiff
books.author: Mori Ōgai
books.synopsis: A mother and her two children, fourteen-year-old Anju and twelve-year-old Zushiō, trudge toward their father in the far west, but boatmen lure them aboard and sell them apart: the mother to Sado, the children to the rich bailiff Sanshō at Yura. Worked hard in his household, the siblings plot an escape, and in the end Zushiō's cry restores sight to his blind mother on Sado.

books.title: The Boat on the Takase River
books.author: Mori Ōgai
books.synopsis: On the Takase boat that carries convicts down the river from Kyoto toward exile, the constable Shōbei escorts Kisuke, a condemned man who seems oddly cheerful about leaving. Kisuke tells his story of killing his brother, and Shōbei is left doubting whether it was murder at all as the boat slips on through the dark.

books.title: The Abe Family
books.author: Mori Ōgai
books.synopsis: When Lord Hosokawa Tadatoshi of Kumamoto dies in 1641, his retainers seek permission to follow him in death, a custom with its own unwritten rules. Abe Yaichiemon is refused leave to die, then mocked as a man who clings to life, and he kills himself anyway; his family barricades itself in their house and is attacked by the clan's troops.

books.title: Li Ling
books.author: Atsushi Nakajima
books.synopsis: After his small army is crushed by the Xiongnu, the Han general Li Ling is taken alive, and the furious Emperor Wu massacres his family. Cut off in the steppe, Li Ling weighs exile against his old comrade Su Wu's loyalty, while the court historian Sima Qian, castrated for defending him, pours himself into his great history.

books.title: Meijinden
books.author: Atsushi Nakajima
books.synopsis: Kichang of Handan sets out to become the greatest archer under heaven, training first to never blink and to see a louse as large as a horse under the master Fei Wei. Sent on to the ancient hermit Ganying, who shoots a kite from the sky with an unstrung bow, he returns an expressionless old man who forgets what a bow even is.

books.title: Under the Cherry Trees
books.author: Motojirō Kajii
books.synopsis: A narrator tells a silent companion that corpses must be buried under every cherry tree in full bloom, since beauty so perfect is unbearable otherwise. Roots, he imagines, drink up the crystalline fluid of the decay, and the grisly vision finally frees him to enjoy the blossoms.

books.title: The Nose
books.author: Ryūnosuke Akutagawa
books.synopsis: The priest Zenchi Naigu has a nose five or six inches long that dangles below his chin, and he has fretted over it all his life. A disciple's method of boiling and treading it shortens it at last, but the people around him laugh more than ever, and he longs for his old nose back.

books.title: Yam Gruel
books.author: Ryūnosuke Akutagawa
books.synopsis: A mocked, red-nosed low official in the household of the Regent Mototsune dreams only of eating his fill of yam gruel. The warrior Toshihito carries him off to Tsuruga, sends a fox ahead with a message, and sets a feast before him, but the poor man's appetite fails once the dream comes true.

books.title: Matasaburo the Wind Imp
books.author: Kenji Miyazawa
books.synopsis: A red-haired boy named Saburo appears one stormy September morning at a one-room mountain schoolhouse, and the village children come to suspect he is the wind spirit Matasaburo. When the gales return, he vanishes as suddenly as he came, leaving only his teacher's word that his father's molybdenum mine is closing.

books.title: The Restaurant of Many Orders
books.author: Kenji Miyazawa
books.synopsis: Two pompous city hunters in British uniforms, lost in the mountains after their dogs drop dead, stumble upon the Wildcat House restaurant. Each door bears a more peculiar request, until they realize that they are the meal.

books.title: Gauche the Cellist
books.author: Kenji Miyazawa
books.synopsis: Gauche, the worst player in a cinema orchestra, is bullied by his conductor and practises all night in his ruined watermill. A cat, a cuckoo, a baby raccoon and a mother mouse visit in turn, and by serving them he finds his playing transformed before the big concert.

books.title: Villon's Wife
books.author: Osamu Dazai
books.synopsis: The wife of Otani, a drunken, dissolute poet, goes to work at a small Nakano restaurant after her husband steals money from its owners. Told in her own voice, she finds a lightness in the squalor and tells him it doesn't matter if they are monsters, so long as they stay alive.

books.title: Schoolgirl
books.author: Osamu Dazai
books.synopsis: A teenage girl's single day, from waking up to going to bed, is told in a restless stream of moods: the commuter train, school, housework, and a quiet evening reading to her mother. She is sharp, self-mocking and unsure which of her selves is real.

books.title: Tsugaru
books.author: Osamu Dazai
books.synopsis: Commissioned to write a regional guide, Dazai spends three weeks in spring circling the Tsugaru peninsula at the northern tip of Honshu. He drinks crab and apple wine with old friends in Kanita, trudges to windswept Tappi, and finally seeks out Take, the nursemaid who raised him.

books.title: An Encouragement of Learning
books.author: Fukuzawa Yukichi
books.synopsis: Opening with 'Heaven did not create one man above another,' Fukuzawa argues in a series of plain-spoken essays that only practical learning separates the wise from the foolish. He urges commoners and samurai alike to seek independence of body and mind, since a nation's independence rests on its people's.

books.title: The Autobiography of Fukuzawa Yukichi
books.author: Fukuzawa Yukichi
books.synopsis: Fukuzawa dictates the story of his life, from a poor samurai childhood in Nakatsu through Dutch studies in Osaka, voyages to America and Europe, and the founding of Keio. He tells it with a blunt, funny disregard for old-fashioned manners as he helps drag Japan into the modern world.

books.title: An Inquiry into the Good
books.author: Nishida Kitarō
books.synopsis: Nishida, teaching at a Kanazawa high school, builds a philosophy on 'pure experience,' the unbroken moment before subject and object divide. From that base he works through the nature of reality, the good as the unity of the self, and religion as the deepest union with God.

books.title: The Silver Spoon
books.author: Naka Kansuke
books.synopsis: A grown man opens a small box and finds the little silver spoon he pried from his mother's cabinet as a sickly child, and the memories pour out. Raised by a doting aunt who tells him tales and has him recite poems at bedtime, he drifts through shrines, festivals, schoolyard bullying and first friendships.

books.title: The Sumida River
books.author: Nagai Kafū
books.synopsis: Rogetsu, a failed haikai master, watches his nephew Chokichi pine for Oito, a childhood sweetheart now training as a geisha, while the boy's mother pushes him toward a respectable business life. Chokichi drifts through the back streets of Asakusa and the Sumida riverside until a flood and a fever bring the story to a hospital door.

mentions.mentioned: The Adventure of the Dancing Men
mentions.author: Arthur Conan Doyle
mentions.note: I have studied ciphers a bit before. I may not be Sherlock Holmes, but even I know a hundred and sixty or so ways of writing in code. (See The Adventure of the Dancing Men)*

mentions.author: Edgar Allan Poe
mentions.note: If this were English, French or German, it would be easy enough just to look for the letter e, as in Poe's The Gold-Bug, but unfortunately this is surely Japanese. Just to be safe I tried a bit of Poe-style deciphering, but it solved nothing.*

mentions.author: Hirotsu Ryuro
mentions.note: From seven o'clock to seven-thirty you leaned on the small desk in your bedroom and read a novel. It was a short story collection by Hirotsu Ryuro, and of it you finished only 'Henmeden'.*

mentions.source: The Strange Tale of Panorama Island
mentions.author: Etienne Cabet
mentions.note: Among such works he was drawn more to Morris's News from Nowhere than to Cabet's Voyage in Icaria, and more than to Morris, to Edgar Poe's The Domain of Arnheim.*

mentions.source: The Strange Tale of Panorama Island
mentions.author: William Morris
mentions.note: Among such works he was drawn more to Morris's News from Nowhere than to Cabet's Voyage in Icaria, and more than to Morris, to Edgar Poe's The Domain of Arnheim.*

mentions.source: The Strange Tale of Panorama Island
mentions.author: Edgar Allan Poe
mentions.note: Among such works he was drawn more to Morris's News from Nowhere than to Cabet's Voyage in Icaria, and more than to Morris, to Edgar Poe's The Domain of Arnheim.*

mentions.source: The Strange Tale of Panorama Island
mentions.author: Edgar Allan Poe
mentions.note: Many of you, dear readers, have probably read Poe's short story The Premature Burial, and know well the horror of being buried alive while only apparently dead.*

"The Arabian Nights is, on the whole, a book for adults to read. What you children have is just a collection of the stories fit for children to read, picked out from it." Kaname explains to his son, who is peering at the illustrations.*

mentions.author: William Shakespeare
mentions.note: Burton's footnote reads: "Even here the coarseness is no greater than in plays written for our own old stage, such as Shakespeare's Henry V. Besides, tales like these Nights are not meant to be read aloud or recited before mixed company."*

mentions.author: Monzaemon Chikamatsu
mentions.note: Kaname vaguely remembered that the Gidayu version of The Love Suicides at Amijima was not Chikamatsu's original but a rewrite by Hanji or someone, and that this line must come from the original; the old man praised the puppet-play texts, saying "today's novels are nowhere near them."*

mentions.author: Charles Darwin
mentions.note: The paper Dr. Masaki submitted then, Dr. Saito predicted, would shake the scholarly world as much as Darwin's On the Origin of Species or Einstein's Principle of Relativity, or even more: it was the Treatise on the Brain.*

mentions.author: Takizawa Bakin
mentions.note: A young man who can calmly answer whether that girl is beautiful is either a worn-out playboy or a descendant of the impotent men who appear in Nansō Satomi Hakkenden and the Water Margin.*

mentions.author: Shi Nai'an
mentions.note: A young man who can calmly answer whether that girl is beautiful is either a worn-out playboy or a descendant of the impotent men who appear in Hakkenden and the Water Margin.*
As for the monk's name, Shōkū, it sounds Tendai, so he probably read something like the Lotus Sutra and grasped this principle from it.*

mentions.author: Rainer Maria Rilke
mentions.note: A small parcel had arrived: Rilke's Requiem for a Friend, ordered long ago, forwarded from place to place with two or three other books. That night, by the fireplace, listening now and then to the wind, I began to read it.*

The Lady of the Yokohagi house began copying the Sutra on the Praise of the Pure Land at that time; the gift of her father's that most enriched the girl's heart was this newly translated Amida Sutra in one scroll.*
Behind the curtained dais came two scrolls apparently copied in a woman's hand: the Lotus Sutra of Lady Tachibana, her great-grandmother, and the Treatise on Yue Yi of the present Empress Dowager.*

They say she was copying the Amida Sutra a thousand times before she left home, that she had practised on the Treatise on Yue Yi and her brother's chronicle of Gangōji, and that she learned the Classic of Filial Piety when she was this small.*
A true woman scholar, she is; one like you, wasting himself on the Chu Ci and on tales, cannot go near her.*

mentions.author: Takizawa Bakin
mentions.note: It may sound like something out of a novel, but it must be like Hamaji in Nansō Satomi Hakkenden, slipping out late at night past her parents' eyes because Shino leaves at dawn. How strange! My own circumstances are like Shino's too: parted from my parents in childhood, raised in the Shigisawa house, betrothed to their daughter.*

mentions.author: Shi Nai'an
mentions.note: "When it comes to this, brute force counts for more than money. Surely this is a scene straight out of the Water Margin? To protect a nation's interests and rights, international law is really worth nothing; what matters is military strength."*

mentions.author: Anonymous
mentions.note: "Some rebellion broke out, and someone petitioned the throne: no need to send an army, just send one general to the river and have him read the Classic of Filial Piety to the rebels, and they will vanish on their own. You laugh at that, but Yusa is in all earnest reading the Classic of Filial Piety, bled every other month by a lender who takes forty percent off the top."*

mentions.author: Ivan Turgenev
mentions.note: This is the opening passage of a short story written by Turgenev and translated by Futabatei under the title "Aibiki" (The Tryst). It is largely thanks to the power of that subtle landscape writing that I came to appreciate woods of fallen leaves.*

Beside the Iruma district the old map is annotated: "Kotesashihara and Kumegawa are old battlefields; the Taiheiki records that in the fifth month of Genkō 3 the Genji and Heike fought at Kotesashihara thirty times in one day," which must refer to this area.*

mentions.author: Gerhart Hauptmann
mentions.note: By some association he suddenly remembered Hauptmann's Lonely Lives. Before things came to this he had thought of making that play her daily lesson, wanting to teach her the heart and sorrow of Johannes Vockerat.*

mentions.author: Ivan Turgenev
mentions.note: He did not go so far as to teach her Lonely Lives, but he once taught her Turgenev's short story First Love. In the lamplit study, as he explained the passage where the hero reads First Love aloud to his former sweetheart, even his voice trembled.*

mentions.author: Ivan Turgenev
mentions.note: For one hour each morning, from nine to ten, he explained Turgenev's novels, and Yoshiko sat slantwise at her desk under his shining eyes, listening to the long, long tale of On the Eve. How deeply Elena's fierce feelings, strong will and sad, tragic end moved her.*

mentions.author: Ivan Turgenev
mentions.note: Fate, life: Turgenev's Punin and Baburin, which he had once taught Yoshiko, rose in Tokio's mind. The meaning of life as drawn by that great Russian writer struck him in the chest as if for the first time.*

mentions.author: Anonymous
mentions.note: The study was four and a half mats. On the big magnolia-wood desk lit by a lamp, the magazines Myojo and Bungei Club, the Man'yoshu and the collected works of Ichiyo lay scattered in a jumble.*

mentions.author: Anonymous
mentions.note: People streamed through the village. Without quite meaning to, he recalled the Man'yoshu and its courtship gatherings at the kagai ground. Every man walked with a partner, talking lewdly without a care.*

mentions.author: Shimazaki Tōson
mentions.note: That night Seizo thought about many things until late. He took out his battered copy of Toson's Wakanashu, its binding coming apart, and read on and on.*

mentions.author: Shimazaki Tōson
mentions.note: On the desk in the main hall lay Midaregami, Ochiumeshu, Musashino, and the thin copy of Enoch Arden that the priest had read when he went to Waseda.*

mentions.author: Yosano Akiko
mentions.note: On the desk in the main hall lay Tangled Hair (Midaregami), Ochiumeshu, Musashino, and the thin copy of Enoch Arden that the priest had read when he went to Waseda.*

mentions.author: Alfred Tennyson
mentions.note: On the desk in the main hall lay Midaregami, Ochiumeshu, Musashino, and the thin copy of Enoch Arden that the priest had read when he went to Waseda.*

mentions.author: Kunikida Doppo
mentions.note: Tired of marking daily grades, Seizo took Musashino out of his bundle and read it eagerly, like a man thirsty for fresh taste. The author's feelings in Unforgettable People matched his own.*

mentions.author: Kunikida Doppo
mentions.note: Tired of marking daily grades, Seizo took Musashino out of his bundle and read it eagerly. The author's feelings in Unforgettable People, the shower in the woods of the Musashino outskirts, the young teacher boarding by the moonlit watermill bridge, all resembled his own.*

mentions.author: Ruiko Kuroiwa
mentions.note: He had lost interest in everything, and even Ruiko's Gankutsuo, which he had loved reading, he gave up halfway.*

mentions.author: Ozaki Kōyō
mentions.note: Seventh: still recovering from illness and a boil, so I postponed returning to school. I started Koyo and Shuto's Kanbotan but gave up. Ninth: finished reading Kanbotan tonight, a story of agony within tragedy that follows sin, and the heroine Luisa's devoted attachment.*
From Ishikawa came the usual attacks on Myojo, and on purpose he sent a pamphlet called Bundan Shomakyo, which exposed the private lives of the poet couple in Shibuya.*

mentions.author: Natsume Sōseki
mentions.note: Then Natsume Kinnosuke began to write novels. Kanai read them with great interest and felt an itch to write himself, but when things like "I Am Also a Cat" and "I Am a Dog" appeared in answer to Natsume's "I Am a Cat," he grew thoroughly sick of the idea and ended up writing nothing.*

mentions.author: Émile Zola
mentions.note: Such a suspicion had crossed his mind when he read Zola's novels as well. It was in Germinal and the like, where he describes the people of a workers' settlement at the extreme of hardship and a passage in which someone goes to peep at a man and woman at a rendezvous, that he had thought so.*

mentions.author: Wilhelm Jerusalem
mentions.note: One day Kanai saw a student in the classroom holding a small book, Jerusalem's Introduction to Philosophy. After the lecture he picked it up and asked what kind of book it was. The student said it had come into the bookshop and he had bought it thinking it might serve as a reference, and Kanai borrowed it and read it that evening.*

mentions.author: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
mentions.note: Rousseau's Confessions is a book that holds back nothing, with remarkable frankness. When he forgot what he had been taught as a child, the pastor's daughter would catch him and spank him, and it felt so wonderful that he pretended not to know things so that she would spank him.*

mentions.author: Friedrich Theodor Vischer
mentions.note: Later, while I was reading Theodor Vischer's Cynismus, I thought of Wanikuchi the whole time. The word cynic comes from the Greek kyon, a dog; a doglike person is one who, as a dog loves to thrust its nose into filth, cannot be satisfied until he has made everything dirty.*

mentions.author: Victor Hugo
mentions.note: When I read Victor Hugo's The Hunchback of Notre-Dame (Notre Dame) and came across the little girl with the jewel-like name of Emeraude, I remembered that girl in Kanda dancing the kappore under the umbrella, and thought she must have been much the same sort of creature.*

mentions.author: Tamenaga Shunsui
mentions.note: He felt as if he were Tanjirō of Shunshoku Umegoyomi, and thought how pleasant it would be to be adored by a girl like Ochō; this notion first stirred in him during this period, when he read lending-library romances.*

One day I saw a Chinese-bound book peeking out from under the master's desk, and it was the Jin Ping Mei. I had read only Bakin's Kinpeibai, but I knew the Chinese-printed Jin Ping Mei was quite different, and thought the master was not to be taken lightly.*

mentions.author: Li Yu
mentions.note: There is an outrageous obscene book by a Chinese author, The Carnal Prayer Mat (Rouputuan), and, as is typical of the Chinese, it tacks a moral of divine retribution onto its plot. It is truly a foolish book, in which the hero Weiyangsheng, worried that a certain part of his body is too small, goes about peeking at people urinating.*

mentions.author: Han Fei
mentions.note: I knew Wanikuchi's character well. He bowed to no authority, and because he held nothing sacred, those around him sometimes suffered for it. I thought him cold-hearted, and the fact that he had studied the Chinese classics and always kept the Han Feizi on his desk probably contributed to that.*

mentions.author: Kikuchi Sankei
mentions.note: Beside Bitō Eiichi I read the Seisetsurō Shishō. One day, as we were reading it together, there was a poem about Tekona of Mama, and I suddenly remembered something and asked him whether his mother was not his real one.*

mentions.author: Kikuchi Sankei
mentions.note: I borrowed from Eiichi and read the Seisetsurō Shishō, and then I read the Honchō Gushō Shinshi. Then, because new pieces by Sankei were coming out, I went to Asakusa and bought the Kagetsu Shinshi and read that too; the two of us made poems and wrote little pieces in Chinese for fun.*

mentions.author: Li Zhen
mentions.note: Since I had made friends who were scholars of Chinese learning, I read the Jiandeng Yuhua, I read the Yanshan Waishi, I read the Qingshi. The naive romances of young men and women written in such books made me terribly envious and jealous.*

mentions.author: Chen Qiu
mentions.note: After I first read the Umegoyomi on a borrowed copy, I made friends who were scholars of Chinese learning, and I read the Jiandeng Yuhua, I read the Yanshan Waishi, I read the Qingshi, and the naive romances in these books left me envious and jealous.*

mentions.author: Feng Menglong
mentions.note: I read the Jiandeng Yuhua, I read the Yanshan Waishi, I read the Qingshi; the naive romances of young men and women in such books were painfully enviable to me, since I had not been born handsome and so this beautiful thing was an unreachable ideal.*

mentions.author: Sima Qian
mentions.note: Later generations know Sima Qian as the author of the Shiji, a great name, but at the time the Grand Historian Sima Qian was a mere minor clerk of letters. His father's deathbed scene was described in detail by his son's own brush in the last chapter of the Records of the Grand Historian.*

mentions.author: Confucius
mentions.note: His plan for a history was unlike any earlier history. As a standard of moral judgment he held up the Spring and Autumn Annals, but as a history that conveyed facts he found it thoroughly unsatisfying. He wanted more facts, facts over lessons.*

When it came to the Zuo Zhuan and the Guoyu, there were certainly facts, and the skill of narration in the Zuo Zhuan could only be admired; but there was no inquiry into the individual people who made those events.*

He wanted more facts, facts over lessons. With the Zuo Zhuan and the Guoyu there are facts indeed, but there is no inquiry into the individual people behind them, and their portrayal within events, though vivid, lacks any investigation of their backgrounds.*

mentions.author: Ban Gu
mentions.note: The Book of Han records that, to treat Su Wu's wound, the Xiongnu dug a pit, lit a fire in it, laid the wounded man over it and trod on his back to draw out the blood.*

mentions.author: Eve Curie
mentions.note: Standing still in the same pose, I suddenly crave money. If I had ten yen it would do. Of all the books, I most want to read 'Madame Curie.' Then I find myself wishing that Mother will live a long life.*

mentions.mentioned: A Strange Tale from East of the River
mentions.author: Nagai Kafu
mentions.note: While I tend the bath, sitting on a mandarin-orange crate by the flickering coal fire, I finish my homework, and then reread 'A Strange Tale from East of the River.' What it describes is not ugly or dirty at all, but here and there I notice the author's affectation, and it feels old and uncertain.*

mentions.author: Edmondo De Amicis
mentions.note: Tonight, after the massage, I read a little of 'Heart' to Mother as a bonus. Whenever I read it, I get the same feeling I had as a small child, and my own heart feels honest and clean. Mother cried, head bowed, at the parts about Enrico and Garrone.*

mentions.author: Joseph Kessel
mentions.note: The other day I was reading Kessel's 'Belle de Jour' when Mother quietly took the book from me and glanced at the cover. She looked very gloomy but said nothing and handed it straight back, and I no longer felt like reading on.*

mentions.author: Osamu Dazai
mentions.note: My life during those four years in Aomori is described in some detail in my early novel 'Memories.' The following is a passage from my own work, 'Memories'.*

mentions.author: Tachibana Nankei
mentions.note: The Toyuki of Tachibana Nankei, the Kyoto physician, published in the Kansei era, says: 'Since the heavens and earth were opened there has never been a time as peaceful as now.' His Toyuki and Seiyuki are counted among the great works of the Edo period.*

mentions.mentioned: The Narrow Road to the Deep North
mentions.author: Matsuo Basho
mentions.note: In Basho's 'The Narrow Road to the Deep North' he writes at the departure, 'thoughts of a journey of three thousand miles weigh upon my heart,' yet even that reached only Hiraizumi, the southern tip of today's Iwate.*

mentions.author: Anonymous
mentions.note: Oh, there were towns even in such a place, I thought, and sighed. It felt like the 'hidden marsh' that appears so often in the Man'yoshu and similar works.*

mentions.author: Anonymous
mentions.note: The Konjaku Monogatari records that Abe no Yoritoki crossed over to Manchuria and what he saw there; taken together with the archaeological and folkloric evidence, this should not be dismissed as a mere tale.*

mentions.author: Confucius
mentions.note: Among the rules said to be Basho's for travellers there was one against drinking for pleasure, and The Analects saying that wine has no set measure but must not reach disorder; I didn't obey it either, and I drank heavily.*

mentions.author: Takeuchi Unpei
mentions.note: According to the 'General History of Aomori Prefecture' by Takeuchi Unpei, a man of Hirosaki, the shore at Kanita was once a source of iron sand, which was refined for use when Hirosaki Castle was built in the Keicho era.*

mentions.author: O no Yasumaro
mentions.note: A man who can recite Japan's Kojiki from memory but does not know today's price of rice should be called ignorant in the learning of everyday life.*

mentions.author: Francis Wayland
mentions.note: In a book called The Elements of Moral Science, written by an American named Wayland, there is a discussion of the freedom of a person's body and mind; the gist of the argument is that each person's self belongs to himself.*

mentions.author: Kaibara Ekken
mentions.note: The book Greater Learning for Women says: 'A woman has three obediences: in youth she obeys her parents, once married her husband, and in old age her sons.'*

mentions.author: Guo Jujing
mentions.note: Stories urging filial piety have been very numerous in Japan and China since ancient times, beginning with the Twenty-Four Paragons of Filial Piety, and the other writings are too many to count.*

mentions.author: Sugita Genpaku
mentions.note: Japan's civilization first came from Korea and China, then was polished by our own people's efforts into its modern shape; Western learning has distant roots, reaching back to the Horeki era (see the printed book Rangaku Koto Hajime).*

mentions.author: John Stuart Mill
mentions.note: Today it seems almost natural that men attend to affairs outside and women manage the home, but Stuart Mill wrote The Subjection of Women, attempting to break this age-old, seemingly fixed custom.*

mentions.author: Zuo Qiuming
mentions.note: Afterwards I attended lectures on other Chinese texts, and then studied alone, history first; I was especially fond of the Zuo Zhuan, and while most students quit after three or four of its fifteen volumes, I read it all, about eleven times, and memorized the interesting parts.*

mentions.author: Sima Qian
mentions.note: For history I read the Records of the Grand Historian first, then the Book of Han and the Book of Later Han, the Jin history, the Five Dynasties and the like.*

mentions.author: Ban Gu
mentions.note: For history I read the Records of the Grand Historian first, then the Book of Han and the Book of Later Han, the Jin history, the Five Dynasties and the like.*
Then I listened to lectures on the Mengqiu, the Shishuo Xinyu, the Zuo Zhuan, the Zhan Guo Ce, Laozi and Zhuangzi.*

mentions.mentioned: A New Account of the Tales of the World
mentions.author: Liu Yiqing
mentions.note: Then I listened to lectures on the Mengqiu, A New Account of the Tales of the World, the Zuo Zhuan, the Zhan Guo Ce, Laozi and Zhuangzi.*

mentions.author: Confucius
mentions.note: At Master Shiraishi's school I studied the classics above all: the Analects and Mencius of course, and the whole range of commentary on the meaning of the classics.*

mentions.author: Mencius
mentions.note: While the others were reading the Classic of Poetry or the Book of Documents, I was doing recitation of Mencius.*

mentions.author: traditional, compiled c. 11th-7th century BC
mentions.note: The master was particularly fond of the Classic of Poetry and the Book of Documents, and I truly received his lectures on them and read them well.*
The master was particularly fond of the Classic of Poetry and the Book of Documents, and I truly received his lectures on them and read them well.*

mentions.author: Zhuang Zhou
mentions.note: I of course studied the Zuo Zhuan, the Classic of Poetry and the Book of Documents, and even odd, interesting works such as Laozi and Zhuangzi, hearing the teacher's lectures and studying them myself.*

mentions.author: Laozi
mentions.note: I of course studied the Classic of Poetry and the Book of Documents, and even odd, interesting works such as the Tao Te Ching and Zhuangzi, hearing the teacher's lectures and studying them myself.*

mentions.author: Anonymous
mentions.note: Among the library was a set of thirteen volumes of the I Ching with annotations, with Ito Togai's own handwritten notes in the margins, a splendid thing that my late father had bought in Osaka and prized.*

mentions.author: Fukuzawa Yukichi
mentions.note: Back in Japan I took those notes as a base, examined many more original books, and wove together what I remembered, and so Conditions in the West came to be.*
I had a copy of Chambers's Political Economy, and when I mentioned it to an influential finance official he was delighted and asked for at least a table of contents, so I set about translating it.*

mentions.author: Fukuzawa Yukichi
mentions.note: I translated a book on bookkeeping, Chōai no Hō, early after the Restoration, and every bookkeeping manual in the world today follows my translation's examples.*

mentions.mentioned: Guide to Travel in the West
mentions.author: Fukuzawa Yukichi
mentions.note: I had no choice but to retire at once as ordered, and during that time I was writing a book called Guide to Travel in the West.*
The passage discussed how light relates to sight, with two candles and the shadows they cast, quite a difficult part, and it should be in the translated book Seiri Hatsumō that Shimamura translated.*

mentions.author: Confucius
mentions.note: That the mean is good is Aristotle's view, and in the East it also appears in the book The Doctrine of the Mean.*

mentions.author: Plato
mentions.note: In his famous work The Republic, Plato equates the organization of the human mind with the organization of the state, and says that the state governed by reason is the highest good for both state and individual.*

mentions.author: Plato
mentions.note: In his famous Symposium, Plato says that 'love is the longing of that which is lacking to return to its original wholeness.'*

mentions.author: Yuien
mentions.note: So the Tannisho also says: 'Even the nembutsu I utter, striving in my own heart for rebirth, I do for my own sake.'*

mentions.author: J. R. Illingworth
mentions.note: A man named Illingworth, in a work titled Personality, Human and Divine, gives self-consciousness, freedom of will and love as the three elements of personality.*

mentions.author: Oscar Wilde
mentions.note: Here I cannot help recalling a passage from Oscar Wilde's De Profundis.*

mentions.author: William James
mentions.note: Just as a geometer imagines one triangle and uses it to stand for all triangles, the representative element of a concept is, when present, only a kind of feeling (James, The Principles of Psychology, Vol. I, Chap. VII).*

mentions.author: William James
mentions.note: Even the so-called fringe of consciousness, once admitted among the facts of immediate experience, brings in the consciousness of relations between experienced facts, just like sensation and perception (James, A World of Pure Experience).*

mentions.author: Wilhelm Wundt
mentions.note: The term experience is not clearly defined; Wundt, for instance, calls knowledge inferred from experience 'indirect experience' and treats physics and chemistry as sciences of indirect experience (Wundt, Grundriss der Psychologie).*

mentions.author: Wilhelm Wundt
mentions.note: As Wundt said, every judgment arises from the analysis of a complex representation (Wundt, Logik, Bd. I, Abs. III, Kap. 1).*

mentions.author: G. F. Stout
mentions.note: Even when it is a reproduction of past consciousness, once it is unified in present consciousness and becomes an element with a new meaning, it can no longer be called identical with the past consciousness (Stout, Analytic Psychology, Vol. II, p. 45).*

mentions.author: G. F. Stout
mentions.note: As when one desperately climbs a cliff, or a musician plays a practiced piece, it may be called a continuous train of perception (Stout, Manual of Psychology, p. 252).*

mentions.mentioned: The World as Will and Representation
mentions.author: Arthur Schopenhauer
mentions.note: This is why the will is always in the present (Schopenhauer, The World as Will and Representation, section 54).*

mentions.author: John Locke
mentions.note: As Locke said that even in demonstrative knowledge each step requires intuitive proof, at the base of every judgment in a chain there must always be a fact of pure experience (Locke, An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, Bk. IV, Chap. II).*

mentions.author: John Dewey
mentions.note: Gore holds that the relation between an image and its meaning is the same as that between a stimulus and its response (Dewey, Studies in Logical Theory).*

mentions.author: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel
mentions.note: Hegel too says that the universal is the soul of the concrete (Hegel, Science of Logic, III, p. 37).*

mentions.author: Henry Sturt
mentions.note: As Schiller and others argue, even an axiom originally developed from practical use, and in its genesis is no different from our mere wishes (Sturt, Personal Idealism, p. 92).*

mentions.author: Wilhelm Jerusalem
mentions.note: As Jerusalem and others hold, the scientific notion that forces act upon the external world must be regarded as an analogy drawn from our own will (Jerusalem, Introduction to Philosophy, section 27).*

mentions.author: Friedrich Schiller
mentions.note: Thunder was the wrath of Zeus on Mount Olympus, and the cuckoo's cry was Philomela's age-old grief (see Schiller, The Gods of Greece).*

mentions.author: Nicholas of Cusa
mentions.note: God is, as Nicholas of Cusa and others said, the negation of everything; nothing affirmable or graspable is God, for what can be grasped is already finite (De Docta Ignorantia, Cap. 24).*

mentions.author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
mentions.note: Like Faust returning to his lonely study late at night after a walk in the fields, following great anguish about life, in quiet nights and a peaceful heart this feeling spontaneously stirs (Goethe, Faust, Part One, Study).*

mentions.author: Josiah Royce
mentions.note: Royce too says, 'The existence of nature is bound up with the belief in the existence of our fellows' (Royce, The World and the Individual, Second Series, Lect. IV).*

mentions.author: Baruch Spinoza
mentions.note: In God knowing is acting and acting is knowing, and reality is directly God's thought and also His will (see Spinoza, Ethics, I, Prop. 17, Scholium).*

mentions.author: Augustine of Hippo
mentions.note: Augustine also says, 'God's will is unchanging; He does not will at one time and not at another, much less reverse an earlier decision later' (The Confessions, XII. 15).*

mentions.author: Storz
mentions.note: Thus what Augustine said, that God beholds all things in an unchanging intuition and that God is at rest in motion and in motion at rest, can also be understood (Storz, Die Philosophie des heiligen Augustinus, section 20).*

mentions.author: William James
mentions.note: One could cite endless such experiences of religious mystics (James, The Varieties of Religious Experience, Lect. XVI, XVII).*

mentions.author: Fujiwara no Sadaie
mentions.note: My aunt knew the whole Hyakunin Isshu by heart and, once in bed, would teach me a poem or two each night in her lonely sing-song voice; I also had a bound copy of the Hyakunin Isshu.*

mentions.author: Wu Cheng'en
mentions.note: Teacher Nakazawa, who told us that marvelous story of Journey to the West, who drew beautiful pictures licking his brush, who was so likable except for the palm-rope whip, I could never see his face again.*

mentions.author: Tamenaga Shunsui
mentions.note: Chokichi read the name of a street on a neighbor's nameplate, and at once recalled Tamenaga Shunsui's Shunshoku Umegoyomi, which he had devoured lately.*
